articles.title: Birth of pine marten kits 'a fantastic sign'
articles.summary: Pine marten babies have been born on Exmoor for the first time in a century, new footage shows.
articles.content:
Pine marten kits have been born on Exmoor for the first time in over a hundred years, new footage has revealed.

A female marten with four babies was captured by camera traps as they explored the woodland.

Nine females and 10 males from Scottish Highlands populations were introduced to the area by the Two Moors Pine Marten Project last year.

Nigel Garnsworthy, restore nature delivery manager at the National Trust, said: "The arrival of pine marten kits on Exmoor is a fantastic sign that these animals are beginning to establish themselves once again in the South West."
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful birth of pine marten kits on Exmoor for the first time in over a century, indicating a positive impact on wildlife restoration and biodiversity. The reintroduction effort involves multiple animals and is part of a broader conservation project, showing significant ecological progress with meaningful benefits for the environment and public awareness.
articles.personality_title: Pine marten babies born on Exmoor for first time in 100 years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Pine martens are small, wild mammals that disappeared from Exmoor, a large area of woodland and moorland in southwest England, over 100 years ago. They are important for the environment because they help keep forests healthy.

**What happened** – Last year, conservationists brought 19 pine martens (9 females and 10 males) from the Scottish Highlands to Exmoor. Recently, cameras captured a female pine marten with four newborn babies exploring the woods. This is the first time in a century that pine marten kits have been born on Exmoor.

**Impact** – This event shows that the pine martens are starting to live and reproduce naturally in the area again. It means the reintroduction project is working well and could help improve the balance of nature on Exmoor. Seeing new baby animals is a clear sign that the environment is becoming healthier.

**What's next step** – Conservation teams will continue to watch the pine martens closely. They hope the population will grow and spread across Exmoor. This success might encourage similar projects in other places to bring back animals that disappeared.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After more than 100 years, pine martens have babies on Exmoor, marking a hopeful step in restoring wildlife to the area.

This process creates a type of polyester, a plastic material, in which the CO2 and bicycloalkane parts alternate regularly. The new polyester can be broken down back into its building blocks and recycled repeatedly without losing quality.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it uses CO2 as a raw material, helping reduce greenhouse gases. The resulting polyesters are high-performance, meaning they can be strong and useful for many applications. Most importantly, they can be recycled in a closed loop, which means less plastic waste and a more sustainable way to produce plastics.

**What's next step** – Scientists will work on scaling up this process to produce these polyesters in larger amounts. They will also explore how to apply this technology to make different kinds of plastics and test their performance in real-world products.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new catalyst enables making strong, recyclable polyesters by directly using CO2 and bicycloalkanes, offering a promising step toward sustainable plastics.

articles.title: How To Recycle a Bicycle
articles.summary:
Between 2020 and 2030, over 12 million electric bikes are expected to be sold in...
The post How To Recycle a Bicycle appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
Between 2020 and 2030, over 12 million electric bikes are expected to be sold in the United States, each with a lithium battery that should never be thrown away. When you add in pedal bikes, old tires, and used tubes, it becomes clear that our clean transportation has an end-of-life issue that most riders rarely consider.

A bicycle is one of the easiest things in your garage to recycle. Its frame is made of steel, aluminum, or titanium; the tires and tubes are rubber, and an e-bike battery contains valuable materials like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper. The main challenge is that most people do not know where these parts should go, so bikes often end up in landfills.

Here is how you can keep every part of a bike, whether regular or electric, in use or in the recycling system.

The Waste Nobody Counts

There is no federal data that tracks bicycles separately. The EPA says Americans created 292.4 million tons of municipal solid waste in 2018, but bikes are hidden in that number. The most-repeated estimate — about 15 million bicycles discarded each year, a figure provided by the junk-removal company 1-800-GOT-JUNK — is a global number. However, it is often repeated as though it applied to the U.S. alone. Investment research firm Harding Loevner counts roughly 170 million bicycles in the United States, replaced on average about every 10 years, which suggests new sales near 17 million units a year. That implies a comparable number leaving service annually, and no one tracks where they go.

It is easier to understand the waste from bike parts. Schwalbe, a tire maker, estimates that nearly 10 million bike inner tubes end up in U.S. landfills each year. These tubes are made of butyl rubber, which can persist in the ground for centuries. On a local scale, Seattle’s Bike Works handles 5,000 to 8,000 donated bikes each year, keeping about 250,000 pounds out of the landfill, and that’s just one nonprofit.

E-bike batteries are emerging as the biggest challenge. The 12 million e-bikes sold mean at least 12 million batteries will need to be dealt with this decade. Since these batteries only last a few years with heavy use, Outside magazine estimates the real number could be 24 to 36 million when replacements are included. Recycling these batteries is important. A 2025 Stanford University study in Nature Communications found that recycling lithium-ion batteries produces less than half the greenhouse gases of mining new metals and uses about a quarter of the water and energy.

Start With Reuse: A Working Bike Beats Scrap

A bike that can still be ridden is much more valuable than as scrap metal. Terry Laibach, a waste-reduction supervisor with New York’s Department of Environmental Conservation, recommends taking bikes to reuse centers, repair cafés, thrift stores, or donation programs before considering the scrap yard. There are national and local networks that make this simple:

Working Bikes in Chicago has given more than 150,000 donated bicycles new life since 1999, redistributing them locally and internationally.

Boston’s Bikes Not Bombs accepts not just whole bikes but parts, accessories, and even cracked frames with usable components, the kind of donation many shops turn away.

Local bike co-ops, such as Community Cycles in Boulder and the Silicon Valley Bicycle Exchange, fix up donated bikes, sell tools and repair time, and accept spare parts. To find one near you, search for “bike co-op” along with your city.

Most reuse nonprofits cannot accept electric bikes because their batteries need special handling and storage. Bike Works, for example, does not take e-bikes and suggests selling yours and donating the money instead. You can sell a working e-bike, give it away, or return it to the manufacturer or a shop that services that brand.

Recycling the Frame and Metal Parts

When a bike can no longer be used, its metal parts are still valuable. Steel, aluminum, and titanium frames can all be recycled as scrap metal. Earth911 recommends removing the tires and tubes, then taking the bare frame to your local scrap yard, where the metal will be recovered and melted down. Chains, cassettes, and other steel or alloy parts can be recycled the same way.

Carbon fiber frames are different. These composite frames are not accepted as scrap metal and remain difficult to recycle. Only a few specialty repair and recycling businesses in the U.S. can handle them. If you have a cracked carbon frame, repairing it is usually better for the environment than throwing it away. Check with a carbon-certified shop before deciding to get rid of it.

Tires and Tubes

Rubber can now be recycled more easily. In December 2024, Trek Bicycle and Liberty Tire Recycling started a nationwide program that lets riders drop off used tires for free at any Trek store in North America. Liberty then turns them into new rubber products.

For inner tubes, Schwalbe’s Cradle-to-Cradle program collects used tubes of any brand through participating bike shops. Once a shop fills a box, they ship it for free, and Schwalbe turns the butyl rubber into new tubes, which already have 20% recycled content. Ask your local shop if they take part, and drop off your used tubes there instead of throwing them away.

Before you recycle, think about upcycling. Companies like Green Guru and Alchemy Goods turn old tubes and tires into bags, wallets, and straps. This gives them a second life and avoids the energy used in recycling.

E-Bike Batteries: The Part That Needs Special Care

Lithium e-bike batteries should never go in household trash or curbside recycling. The EPA warns that these batteries can catch fire if crushed in garbage trucks or sorting machines, and most municipal facilities are not equipped to handle them. This is a real risk. After Seattle banned all batteries from the trash in 2024, the city’s fire department responded to 79 lithium-ion battery fires in two years, many involving e-bikes and e-scooters.

If a battery is swollen, punctured, leaking, hot, or recalled by the manufacturer, it is especially risky. Please refer to Earth911’s guide to handling damaged lithium-ion batteries. Do not put it in a regular battery collection box or drop it off without warning. The good news is that the bike industry built a dedicated pathway. The Battery Network, the nonprofit formerly known as Call2Recycle, runs the Hungry for Batteries program with PeopleForBikes. More than 60 bike-industry brands fund it, including Trek, Specialized, Giant, Pedego, Rad Power, and Super73, plus motor makers Bosch, Shimano, and Yamaha.

For riders, the process is free and simple. Brands pay a recycling fee for each battery, so when your battery reaches the end of its life, you just drop it off at a participating retailer, such as Trek, Rad Power, or REI. Trained staff will package and ship it. According to Forbes, 67% of Americans now live within 10 miles of a drop-off location, and the program collected 60,000 pounds of e-bike batteries in its first year. At the recycling facility, Redwood Materials recovers 95 to 98% of the battery’s materials for use in new cells.

There is one limitation: the program only accepts batteries from participating brands, since those brands pay for recycling. If you have a low-cost or off-brand e-bike, contact the manufacturer for its own take-back program, or bring the battery to a household hazardous waste facility. You can use The Battery Network’s drop-off locator to find the closest site.

What You Can Do

Ride it longer first. Repair beats replacement on every environmental measure. A tune-up, a new chain, or a carbon repair keeps the whole machine in service.

Repair beats replacement on every environmental measure. A tune-up, a new chain, or a carbon repair keeps the whole machine in service. Donate anything rideable. Working Bikes, Bikes Not Bombs, and your local co-op will take whole bikes and usable parts; many accept components other shops reject.

Working Bikes, Bikes Not Bombs, and your local co-op will take whole bikes and usable parts; many accept components other shops reject. Recycle tires and tubes at the shop. Drop worn tires at a Trek store and dead tubes at any Schwalbe-participating shop instead of the trash.

Drop worn tires at a Trek store and dead tubes at any Schwalbe-participating shop instead of the trash. Scrap the bare metal frame. Strip tires and tubes, then take a steel, aluminum, or titanium frame to a scrap-metal yard.

Strip tires and tubes, then take a steel, aluminum, or titanium frame to a scrap-metal yard. Never trash an e-bike battery. Return participating-brand packs through the Hungry for Batteries network; route off-brand or damaged batteries to household hazardous waste.

Return participating-brand packs through the Hungry for Batteries network; route off-brand or damaged batteries to household hazardous waste. Buy with the end in mind. Choose brands enrolled in battery and tire take-back programs, and favor repairable bikes over disposable ones.

articles.personality_title: How to recycle your bike and keep parts out of landfills
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Millions of bicycles, including electric bikes with lithium batteries, are sold in the U.S. each year. Many old bikes and their parts, like tires and batteries, often end up in landfills, creating waste problems that people rarely think about.

**What happened** – Experts and organizations have shared clear ways to recycle or reuse every part of a bike. For example, steel or aluminum frames can be taken to scrap yards, tires and inner tubes can be dropped off at special stores, and electric bike batteries have a new nationwide recycling program called Hungry for Batteries. There are also groups that repair and give old bikes a new life instead of throwing them away.

**Impact** – This is important because bike parts, especially lithium batteries, contain valuable materials and can harm the environment if thrown away incorrectly. Recycling batteries saves energy and water compared to mining new materials. Programs like the one by Trek and Schwalbe make it easy for people to recycle tires and tubes, reducing waste that can last for centuries in landfills.

**What's next step** – People are encouraged to repair bikes instead of replacing them, donate usable bikes and parts to local nonprofits, and use the new recycling programs for batteries and tires. Bike brands are also being urged to join these programs so more batteries can be safely recycled. This helps keep bike materials in use and reduces harmful waste.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By repairing, reusing, and recycling bike parts, especially electric bike batteries, riders can help reduce landfill waste and protect the environment.

articles.title: China’s solar industry is losing money. The country is doubling down anyway.
articles.content:
Cheap, abundant Chinese solar panels have become essential to decarbonizing the global energy system. Without them, the world’s clean energy transition would have arguably been slower and more expensive. But China’s solar manufacturing industry now faces a bizarre problem: oversupply. Chinese solar manufacturers have built far more production capacity than the market can absorb. In fact, China now has enough factories to meet roughly twice the global demand for solar products, according to an analysis by the research firm Rhodium Group. If all newly announced factories get built, the country’s manufacturing capacity could double, further widening the gap between supply and demand.

The market imbalance has put Chinese solar panel makers in a precarious position. Market analysts and company executives say the industry’s central problem — a massive oversupply of panels — has triggered vicious “price wars” between competing companies and sent prices plummeting. In the first quarter of 2026, the country’s solar manufacturers announced $1.5 billion in losses, an extension of roughly three years of continuous unprofitability. Industry behemoths like JinkoSolar and Longi have also been facing slowing installations in China, U.S. trade barriers, and weaker global demand.

“There’s been an enormous amount of price wars internally in China, with companies just slashing prices to very, very low levels,” said Hannah Pitt, director of the energy and climate practice at Rhodium Group.

Chinese officials have spent years trying to curb the cutthroat competition, stem overproduction, and stabilize prices, with little success. For all but the most advanced solar products, prices kept falling, and companies kept building new facilities. Regional governments, which have invested heavily in solar supply chains, have been hesitant to trim local development. Some manufacturers even built illegal factories or produced panels without permits, according to reporting by the South China Morning Post.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“Everyone is wondering how long this can last,” said Martin Schachinger, a solar product wholesaler based in Germany. “Even TaleSun, a manufacturer we expected to go out of the market five years ago, still exists. So, it’s a little bit … spooky.”

China designated solar a strategic industry in 2010, prompting massive public investment. Local governments subsidized manufacturers, while private investors expanded every stage of the supply chain in anticipation of booming global demand. The resulting manufacturing ecosystem allowed Chinese firms to produce extraordinarily cheap solar panels for both domestic and international markets.

But production soon outpaced global demand, triggering a fierce battle as manufacturers slashed prices to win customers. The Chinese government dubbed this self-defeating competition neijuan, meaning “involution,” a term originally coined by Chinese students describing the relentless pressure to succeed with diminishing returns. Involution is a common trend in Chinese industries that receive heavy public support, including other clean energy sectors such as batteries and electric vehicles.

For the United States and the rest of the globe, the oversupply has meant consistent availability of cheap solar panels and components that boosted the adoption of renewable energy. Solar panels provided more electricity in the United States than coal for the first time on record in May, according to analysis of government data by Ember, an energy think tank. Globally, clean power sources, of which solar is the fastest growing, met all new electricity demand around the world in 2025, staving off an increase in fossil fuel generation. It’s helped China, the world’s largest net emitter of greenhouse gases, flatten its emissions growth, too. The country’s emissions appear to have plateaued and could soon peak.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

If Chinese officials correct the oversupply problem, it could cool some of that rapid solar deployment. But experts say China is more focused on advancing its solar industry than rightsizing it, meaning the cheap solar panel prices may continue for years.

Chinese officials have called for “concerted efforts” to rein in solar production as recently as April. But the country’s broader industrial policies and stated goals seem to be leaning away from strict discipline, focusing instead on upgrading solar supply chains to produce more advanced technologies, according to a May report by Rhodium Group. In other words, the oversupply problem isn’t scaring China away from its big bets on solar. In fact, its latest five-year plan signals that China will continue supporting its massive clean energy industries, including solar, “optimizing and upgrading“ those industries rather than clamping down on their oversupply.

“It’s a really interesting moment right now across Chinese industries. Instead of just trying to consolidate, Beijing is pushing industries to go further, to move into more advanced manufacturing,” said Pitt.

The strategy stands in stark contrast to the United States’ steady solar manufacturing growth, which relies on market conditions rather than government support. Over the past year, the Trump administration and Congress have weakened policy incentives for solar, cutting back tax credits expanded in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and impeding solar development on federal land.

But demand for cheap solar has kept the industry growing. Unlike China’s self-sufficient solar empire, U.S. producers can’t meet all domestic demand for solar panels and are still heavily reliant on foreign components, primarily from China. While the U.S. pursues a slower, market-led approach, China has chosen a long-term state strategy that prioritizes manufacturing dominance over near-term profits.

That manufacturing dominance is especially important now that other countries are pushing back against China’s near-monopoly in the industry. The country’s efforts to upgrade its supply chains and move into higher-value products could help it stay ahead as new technologies reshape the solar market and countries attempt to build their own competing industries.

“If a solar company in Europe doesn’t make a joint venture with Chinese companies and use the huge advantages of the Chinese systems, then it won’t be successful,” said Schachinger. “From time to time, Indian manufacturers try to step into the European market, but against Chinese products, they have no advantages, and the prices are higher.”

That means if unsustainable business models or geopolitical tensions don’t spoil the boom, the world will have at least a few more years of low-cost Chinese solar products to supply its decarbonization goals, experts suspect.

“This isn’t over yet,” Pitt said. “I think the data points to prices remaining low for the foreseeable future.”

articles.personality_title: China’s solar industry oversupply keeps prices low and boosts global clean energy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – China has built many factories to make solar panels, more than the world needs. This has caused an oversupply, meaning there are more solar panels available than buyers. 

**What happened** – Chinese solar companies are losing money because they make too many panels and must lower prices to sell them. In early 2026, these companies reported $1.5 billion in losses. Despite this, China continues to build new solar factories and improve technology instead of cutting back production.

**Impact** – The oversupply has made solar panels very cheap worldwide. This helps many countries use more solar energy, which is cleaner than fossil fuels. For example, in the U.S., solar power produced more electricity than coal for the first time. Also, China’s greenhouse gas emissions have stopped growing, partly thanks to cheap solar panels.

**What’s next step** – China plans to keep supporting its solar industry by upgrading technology and expanding production. This may keep solar panel prices low for years. Meanwhile, other countries like the U.S. are growing their solar industries more slowly and depend on imports from China.

**One-sentence takeaway** – China’s large solar panel production is causing losses but also keeping prices low worldwide, helping many countries use cleaner energy faster.

articles.personality_title_es: La sobreproducción solar de China mantiene precios bajos y acelera la energía limpia global
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – China ha construido muchas fábricas para fabricar paneles solares, más de los que el mundo necesita. Esto ha causado un exceso, es decir, hay más paneles solares disponibles que compradores.

**Qué pasó** – Las empresas solares chinas están perdiendo dinero porque producen demasiados paneles y deben bajar los precios para venderlos. A principios de 2026, estas empresas anunciaron pérdidas de 1.500 millones de dólares. A pesar de esto, China sigue construyendo nuevas fábricas y mejorando la tecnología en lugar de reducir la producción.

**Impacto** – El exceso de oferta ha hecho que los paneles solares sean muy baratos en todo el mundo. Esto ayuda a muchos países a usar más energía solar, que es más limpia que los combustibles fósiles. Por ejemplo, en Estados Unidos, la energía solar produjo más electricidad que el carbón por primera vez. Además, las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero de China han dejado de crecer, en parte gracias a los paneles solares baratos.

**Próximo paso** – China planea seguir apoyando su industria solar mejorando la tecnología y aumentando la producción. Esto puede mantener los precios de los paneles solares bajos durante años. Mientras tanto, otros países como Estados Unidos están creciendo su industria solar más lentamente y dependen de importaciones chinas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La gran producción de paneles solares en China causa pérdidas pero también mantiene precios bajos en todo el mundo, ayudando a muchos países a usar energía más limpia más rápido.
